source_evidence.anchor: opening setup beginning 'For a matrix A in R^{m x n}'
source_evidence.observation: The standing setup takes A to be a real m-by-n matrix with m >= n and rank(A) = n, and uses A = (a_1,...,a_n), Q = (q_1,...,q_n), and upper-triangular R.
Algorithm 2 computes s_k = Q_{k-1}^T a_k and v_k = a_k - Q_{k-1}s_k, but computes r_kk by the Pythagorean formula using psi_k = ||a_k||_2 and phi_k = ||s_k||_2, rather than by ||v_k||_2.

source_evidence.anchor: paragraph beginning 'We assume that we are using a floating point arithmetic'
source_evidence.observation: The paper assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic, states fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), |delta| <= epsilon_M, for normalized-range results, and adopts a first-order approximation that neglects O(epsilon_M^2).
The paper defines c_1 and c_2 piecewise, c_3(m,k) = 0.5c_2(m,k), c_4(m,k) = c_2(m,k) + 2c_1(m,k), A_k as the first k columns of A, and kappa_2(R_k) = ||R_k||_2 ||R_k^{-1}||_2.
For the computed Algorithm 2 factors, Theorem 1 assumes c_4(m,k) epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 for every k and defines the residuals by Q_k R_k - A_k = Delta A_k and R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k = E_k.
Outside the assumptions of Theorem 1, phi_k can be at least psi_k, causing Algorithm 2 to break down and produce non-real Q and R.

source_evidence.anchor: Lemma 2 proof beginning 'Using (3), we conclude that R is nonsingular'
source_evidence.observation: The proof uses condition (3) to conclude that R is nonsingular, hence r_kk > 0, and consequently psi_k > phi_k.

source_evidence.anchor: unnumbered display following 'To get (7), we note that'
source_evidence.observation: The passage derives Q_k = (A_k + Delta A_k)R_k^{-1} and gives the exact two-line expansion of I - Q_k^T Q_k in terms of R_k, E_k, A_k, and Delta A_k before taking norms.

binders: Inherited setup: A is in R^{m x n}, with m >= n and rank(A) = n. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: opening matrix setup]

Quantifier order: Algorithm 2 first produces computed Q and R from A; condition (3) is assumed for every k; the conclusions then apply for every k = 1,...,n. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1]

For each such k, A_k and Q_k are m-by-k, R_k is k-by-k, Delta A_k is m-by-k, and E_k is k-by-k; the latter dimensions follow from equations (4)-(5). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (4)-(5)]
hypotheses: The full-rank real-matrix setup is inherited from the paper's opening formulation rather than restated in the displayed identity. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: opening matrix setup]

Q_k and R_k are computed leading factors produced by the Pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt variant, Algorithm 2. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1]
For every k, c_4(m,k) epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (3)]

R_k must be invertible for R_k^{-1} and R_k^{-T} to exist; the theorem states that condition (3) assures nonsingularity, and the proof derives positive diagonal entries. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: paragraph after Theorem 1; PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 nonsingularity argument]
conclusions: Q_k = (A_k + Delta A_k)R_k^{-1}. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: display immediately after 'To get (7), we note that']
I - Q_k^T Q_k = R_k^{-T}(R_k^T R_k - (A_k + Delta A_k)^T(A_k + Delta A_k))R_k^{-1}. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: first line of the unnumbered identity]
I - Q_k^T Q_k = R_k^{-T}(E_k - A_k^T Delta A_k - (Delta A_k)^T A_k - (Delta A_k)^T(Delta A_k))R_k^{-1}. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: second line of the unnumbered identity]
definitions_and_conventions: A_k is the matrix formed from the first k columns of A. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition preceding Theorem 1]
Delta A_k is defined exactly by Q_k R_k - A_k = Delta A_k, and E_k is defined exactly by R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k = E_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (4)-(5)]
The relation Q_k = (A_k + Delta A_k)R_k^{-1} is obtained algebraically from the definition of Delta A_k and invertibility of R_k. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: display preceding the identity]

I must be the k-by-k identity matrix, and R_k^{-T} denotes the transpose of R_k^{-1}; both are dimensionally inferred because the passage does not annotate them explicitly. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: unnumbered identity]
implicit_context: The identity is an unnumbered intermediate step in the appendix proof of Theorem 1, specifically in the derivation of orthogonality bound (7), rather than a separately stated theorem. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: 'To get (7)']

The passage explicitly invokes residual relations (4) and (5): (4) supplies A_k + Delta A_k = Q_k R_k, while (5) supplies E_k = R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (4)-(5); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: opening sentence and identity]

Although presented under Theorem 1's numerical assumptions, the displayed equality itself is an exact algebraic consequence of the two residual definitions and invertibility of R_k. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: complete unnumbered identity]
statement.algorithm_linkage: The enclosing result concerns Algorithm 2, CGS-P: it uses s_k = Q_{k-1}^T a_k, v_k = a_k - Q_{k-1}s_k, psi_k = ||a_k||_2, phi_k = ||s_k||_2, and r_kk = (psi_k - phi_k)^{1/2}(psi_k + phi_k)^{1/2}; it is not the standard r_kk = ||v_k||_2 variant. The identity becomes algorithm-independent once its residual relations and invertibility are assumed. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: unnumbered identity]
numerical_model: The enclosing theorem concerns computed Q_k and R_k in floating-point arithmetic with machine unit epsilon_M. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1]
The stated IEEE model is fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), |delta| <= epsilon_M, restricted to normalized-range results. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: IEEE arithmetic paragraph]

The paper adopts a first-order model using (1+epsilon_M)^{p(n)} = 1 + p(n)epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2) and assumes the O(epsilon_M^2) contribution is insignificant. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: linear-approximation paragraph]

The selected identity contains no fl operation, epsilon_M, inequality, or approximation: it is exact for the computed matrices and their exactly defined residuals. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: unnumbered identity]
error_notions: Delta A_k is the factorization residual or backward perturbation satisfying Q_k R_k = A_k + Delta A_k, with first-order bound ||Delta A_k||_2 <= c_1(m,k)||A_k||_2 epsilon_M. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (4)]
E_k is the normal-equations residual satisfying R_k^T R_k = A_k^T A_k + E_k, with first-order bound ||E_k||_2 <= c_2(m,k)||A_k||_2^2 epsilon_M. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (5)]
I - Q_k^T Q_k is the orthogonality defect; the identity precedes the normwise estimate leading to equation (7). [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: identity and following 'Thus' estimate]
norms: The residual bounds, condition number, and orthogonality bound use ||.||_2. The nearby text does not separately define this norm; its use for matrices as the operator 2-norm and for vectors as the Euclidean norm is conventional and consistent with the algorithm and kappa_2 definition. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition of kappa_2(R_k)]
kappa_2(R_k) is explicitly ||R_k||_2 ||R_k^{-1}||_2, and equation (7) uses its square. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition of kappa_2(R_k) and equation (7)]
The selected two-line identity itself is norm-free; norms enter only in the subsequent inequality. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: identity followed by 'Thus']
constants_and_indexing: For k = 1, c_1(m,1) = 1 and c_2(m,1) = m + 2; for k = 2,...,n, c_1(m,k) = 2 sqrt(2mk) + 2 sqrt(k) and c_2(m,k) = 3.5mk^2 - 1.5mk + 16k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2)]
c_3(m,k) = 0.5c_2(m,k), and c_4(m,k) = c_2(m,k) + 2c_1(m,k). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2)]

The same index k is used for the first k columns A_k and the leading computed factors Q_k and R_k; there is no index offset in the identity. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2 block construction; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition of A_k]
higher_order_terms: The exact expansion explicitly retains the quadratic term -(Delta A_k)^T(Delta A_k); it is not omitted from the identity. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: second line of the unnumbered identity]

The enclosing theorem states its bounds only to within O(epsilon_M^2), following the paper's declared first-order approximation. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: linear-approximation paragraph; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1]

After the exact identity, the norm estimate contains an explicit +O(epsilon_M^2), but the identity itself contains no big-O remainder. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: identity and following norm estimate]
exceptional_values: The stated rounding relation is limited to normalized-range results; the cited setup does not explicitly specify behavior for subnormals, overflow, infinities, or NaNs. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: IEEE arithmetic paragraph]

Condition (3) is used to secure nonsingularity and positive r_kk, so the divisions and inverse matrices occurring in the passage are defined. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: paragraph after Theorem 1; PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 nonsingularity argument]
If the theorem assumptions fail, phi_k >= psi_k can make Algorithm 2's square roots break down and yield non-real factors. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2]

undebatable_constraints: The left side is I - Q_k^T Q_k, not Q_k^T Q_k - I. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: unnumbered identity]
The first right-hand side is conjugated on the left and right by R_k^{-T} and R_k^{-1}, in that order. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: first line of the identity]
E_k has the sign convention E_k = R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (5)]
All three correction terms after E_k are subtracted: A_k^T Delta A_k, (Delta A_k)^T A_k, and (Delta A_k)^T(Delta A_k). [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: second line of the identity]

The quadratic residual product (Delta A_k)^T(Delta A_k) is part of the exact source statement and cannot be silently discarded as higher order. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: second line of the identity]
R_k must be invertible, and all products must have k-by-k result type. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: occurrences of R_k^{-1} and the identity matrix]
The source equality is exact; epsilon_M and O(epsilon_M^2) belong to the surrounding bounds, not to this identity. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: identity and subsequent estimate]

contract_plain_english: For each leading step k of the computed CGS-P factorization, under the inherited full-rank real-matrix setup and the theorem's condition ensuring invertible R_k, define Delta A_k exactly by Q_k R_k - A_k and E_k exactly by R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k. Then Q_k = (A_k + Delta A_k)R_k^{-1}, and the k-by-k orthogonality defect is exactly R_k^{-T}[E_k - A_k^T Delta A_k - (Delta A_k)^T A_k - (Delta A_k)^T(Delta A_k)]R_k^{-1}. The quadratic residual term is explicitly present, and no epsilon_M or big-O truncation belongs to this equality; those enter only when the paper subsequently takes 2-norms to prove bound (7). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (3)-(5); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: unnumbered two-line identity and following estimate]
